evidence.title: Liriodendron
evidence.text: Liriodendron is a genus of two species of characteristically large deciduous trees in the magnolia family (Magnoliaceae).

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: Liriodendron tulipifera—known as the tulip tree, American tulip tree, tuliptree, tulip poplar, whitewood, fiddletree, and yellow-poplar—is the Western Hemisphere representative of the two-species genus "Liriodendron," and the tallest eastern hardwood.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: It is native to eastern North America from Southern Ontario and Illinois eastward to southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, and south to central Florida and Louisiana.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: It can grow to more than 50 m in virgin cove forests of the Appalachian Mountains, often with no limbs until it reaches 25 – in height, making it a very valuable timber tree.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: It is fast-growing, without the common problems of weak wood strength and short lifespan often seen in fast-growing species.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: April marks the start of the flowering period in the southern USA (except as noted below); trees at the northern limit of cultivation begin to flower in June.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: The flowers are pale green or yellow (rarely white), with an orange band on the tepals; they yield large quantities of nectar.

evidence.title: Liriodendron tulipifera
evidence.text: The tulip tree is the state tree of Indiana, Kentucky, and Tennessee.
